strengths: The paper addresses a timely and clearly NLP-relevant topic: evidence-based text generation with LLMs, including citations, attribution, and quotations. The framing is useful because it brings together several related but fragmented lines of work under one umbrella.

The survey covers a substantial body of recent work: 134 papers, 300 reported metrics, 231 datasets, 17 frameworks, and 11 benchmarks. This breadth makes the paper potentially valuable as an entry point for researchers working on grounded generation and citation-aware LLMs.

The proposed taxonomy is practically useful. The distinctions among attribution approach, LLM integration, citation characteristics, and task give readers a structured way to compare methods that are often described using inconsistent terminology.

The evaluation section is one of the stronger parts of the paper. Categorizing metrics by evaluation dimension and evaluation method helps clarify why current work is difficult to compare and supports the paper’s claim that standardization is still lacking.
The paper is generally well organized and readable, with clear research questions, an explicit search process, and informative tables summarizing datasets, frameworks, and benchmarks.
weaknesses: The claim of being a comprehensive survey is weakened by the narrow search string: only title/abstract matches for “large language model” or “llm” combined with “citation”, “attribution”, or “quote”. This likely misses relevant work using terms such as grounded generation, source-aware generation, verifiable generation, provenance, faithful RAG, evidence-supported QA, or retrieval-augmented generation without explicit citation terminology.

The systematic-review methodology lacks important rigor details. The paper does not report exclusion counts by stage, a PRISMA-style flow, inter-annotator agreement, disagreement rates, or quantitative reliability of the coding scheme. Since the taxonomy and counts are central contributions, this limits confidence in the annotations.

The annotation procedure appears only partially independent: screening was independent, but categorization was split between the first two authors with regular reviews. Without double annotation or agreement statistics, the many fine-grained labels, especially for metrics and citation characteristics, may reflect subjective judgment.

Reproducibility is only partially supported. The paper says the annotated dataset and full dataset list are available in a public Git repository, but the manuscript text does not provide an accessible URL or enough detail to reproduce the database queries, deduplication, and coding decisions from scratch.

Several categories would benefit from sharper definitions and boundary cases. For example, distinctions between attribution and citation metrics, post-retrieval vs. in-context attribution, and frameworks vs. benchmarks are plausible but sometimes applied without enough examples of difficult cases.

The discussion section is sensible but somewhat high-level. It mostly restates observed gaps, such as lack of standards and limited parametric attribution, rather than deriving deeper insights from the collected evidence or critically evaluating methodological failure modes in the surveyed literature.

The contribution is useful and sound enough for Findings, but not yet compelling for main-conference acceptance because the novelty is mainly organizational and the central empirical claims depend on a review protocol whose coverage and annotation reliability are not fully demonstrated.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely NLP problem: evidence-based generation with LLMs, including citation, attribution, and quotation, where terminology and evaluation practices are genuinely fragmented.

The manuscript provides a useful high-level taxonomy spanning attribution approach, LLM integration, citation characteristics, and task types, and it consolidates many scattered strands of recent work into one readable structure.

The survey covers a nontrivial body of work: 134 papers, 300 reported metrics, 231 datasets, 17 evaluation frameworks, and 11 benchmarks. The resulting inventories, if released as claimed, could be practically useful to researchers entering the area.

The discussion correctly identifies important field-level issues, especially the lack of standardized evaluation, the dominance of QA-style datasets, and the underdevelopment of explainable citation behavior.
weaknesses: The literature search is too narrow for the paper's broad claims. Searching only title/abstract for “large language model” or “llm” together with “citation”, “attribution”, or “quote” likely misses substantial work under terms such as grounding, provenance, verifiability, factuality, source support, faithful generation, RAG evaluation, and evidence alignment. This undermines the claim of comprehensive coverage.

The systematic review protocol is under-specified. The paper reports that two authors screened and annotated papers, but gives no inter-annotator agreement, disagreement rate, calibration process, exclusion breakdown, PRISMA-style flow, or detailed coding manual. This makes the taxonomy and frequency counts hard to audit.

The evidence is mostly descriptive counting rather than critical synthesis. Many sections define categories and list representative papers, but provide limited comparative analysis of why methods succeed or fail, how evaluation choices affect conclusions, or which research claims are actually supported by reliable evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript itself. The paper says the annotated dataset and full dataset list are in a public Git repository, but the extracted text does not provide a visible URL or enough detail to reproduce the search, deduplication, inclusion, and annotation pipeline from the paper alone.

The taxonomy sometimes appears ad hoc and insufficiently justified. For example, distinctions among post-retrieval, in-context, and in-generation attribution are plausible but not stress-tested against ambiguous cases, and the boundary between citation, attribution, quotation, and broader grounded generation remains somewhat fluid.

The evaluation survey catalogs many metrics but does not deeply assess their validity. Metrics based on NLI, lexical overlap, LLM-as-judge, and retrieval are described, but the paper gives limited guidance on known failure modes, correlation with human verification, domain robustness, or suitability for different evidence granularities.

The contribution is useful but not especially strong as a main-conference survey. The paper is clear and relevant, but its main added value is organization and enumeration rather than a particularly rigorous methodology, new conceptual insight, or decisive synthesis of the field.

strengths: Timely and relevant survey topic: evidence-based text generation, attribution, citation, and quotation are central to current NLP work on trustworthy LLMs, and the paper addresses a real fragmentation in terminology and evaluation practice.

The paper has a broad empirical basis for a survey, covering 134 papers, 300 metrics, 17 evaluation frameworks, 231 datasets, and 11 benchmarks, with a clear attempt to make the annotated dataset publicly available.

The proposed taxonomy is useful and reasonably well organized, separating attribution approach, LLM integration, citation characteristics, and task. The distinction among post-retrieval, post-generation, in-generation, and in-context attribution is especially helpful for situating recent RAG-adjacent work.

The evaluation section is one of the strongest parts of the paper. Classifying metrics by evaluation dimensions and methods gives readers a practical map of a confusing literature and supports the paper's claim that evaluation is fragmented.
The manuscript is clearly written, well scoped for ACL/NLP, and generally easy to follow. Figures and tables summarize the main findings effectively.
weaknesses: The systematic-review methodology is under-specified in important ways. The paper does not report inter-annotator agreement, exclusion counts by screening stage, examples of difficult inclusion/exclusion decisions, or enough detail on how annotation conflicts were resolved. This weakens reproducibility and confidence in the taxonomy counts.

The search query is quite narrow: requiring title/abstract matches for both LLM terminology and one of citation/attribution/quote may miss relevant work framed as grounding, provenance, verifiability, factuality, evidence support, source use, or RAG evaluation. The paper should better justify recall and discuss likely omissions.

The taxonomy is useful but not always critically validated. Some categories overlap conceptually, and the paper gives limited evidence that the scheme is stable across annotators or superior to alternative organizations of the field.

The survey is more descriptive than analytical in several places. It catalogs approaches and metrics well, but offers less comparative synthesis about which methods work, under what assumptions, and where evidence is strongest or weakest.

The discussion of limitations is relatively thin for a survey. More explicit threats to validity, coverage limitations, publication-bias concerns, and caveats about arXiv/preprint inclusion would improve the paper's soundness.

The contribution supports a strong Findings-level recommendation and is close to main-conference quality, but the methodological transparency and depth of critical synthesis currently limit confidence in a clear Conference recommendation.

strengths: Timely and relevant survey topic: evidence-based LLM generation with citations, attribution, and quotations is central to current NLP concerns around hallucination, verifiability, and trustworthy generation.
The paper is well scoped and useful as a synthesis resource, covering 134 papers, 300 evaluation metrics, 19 frameworks, 231 datasets, and 11 benchmarks.

The taxonomy is clear and practically helpful, separating attribution approach, citation characteristics, task, and LLM integration in a way that can support comparison across otherwise fragmented work.

The methodology is more rigorous than many survey papers: it reports a PRISMA-style flow, explicit inclusion criteria, database coverage, sensitivity analysis, and inter-annotator agreement for screening and taxonomy annotation.

The evaluation section is a strong contribution, especially the organization of metrics by dimensions and methods, plus the concrete guidance on when attribution, citation, correctness, retrieval, relevance, preservation, and linguistic quality should be evaluated.
The paper is clearly written, well organized, and includes extensive appendices that make the survey navigable and relatively reproducible.
weaknesses: The main contribution is primarily taxonomic and descriptive; the paper offers less deep critical analysis of why methods succeed or fail, how assumptions differ across tasks, or which research directions are most technically promising beyond broad high-level themes.

The search strategy is narrow, relying on one main title/abstract query centered on “large language model/llm” and “citation/attribution/quote”; the sensitivity analysis finds five additional relevant papers but does not incorporate them into the corpus, which weakens the claim of comprehensive coverage.

Screening and annotation were split between two annotators, with only subsets double-annotated for agreement. This is acceptable for a large survey, but leaves some residual uncertainty about consistency across the full 134-paper dataset.
The survey does not appear to perform a quality appraisal of included papers, so counts and trends may treat mature, validated systems similarly to preliminary arXiv work or position papers.

Some category boundaries seem potentially ambiguous, such as attribution vs citation evaluation, post-retrieval vs in-context settings, and framework vs benchmark distinctions; the paper reports agreement but could better justify difficult borderline decisions with examples.
The public repository is important for reproducibility, but the manuscript text as provided shows only a truncated GitHub URL, making it hard to verify availability from the paper itself.

For main-conference strength, the work would benefit from more comparative insight: e.g., identifying failure modes in existing evaluation, mapping metric validity to use cases, or giving stronger evidence that the proposed taxonomy improves analysis over prior surveys.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant NLP topic: evidence-based text generation with LLMs, including citations, attribution, quotations, retrieval-augmented generation, and evaluation practices.

The manuscript assembles a sizable survey corpus of 134 papers and reports useful descriptive resources: taxonomy dimensions, counts over attribution approaches, citation characteristics, tasks, metrics, frameworks, benchmarks, and datasets.
The PRISMA-style reporting, inclusion criteria, sensitivity analysis, and inter-annotator agreement table are positive attempts at methodological transparency for a survey paper.

The evaluation section is potentially useful: organizing 300 metrics into dimensions such as attribution, citation, correctness, relevance, retrieval, and linguistic quality could help practitioners select evaluation protocols.
weaknesses: The reproducibility case is weak. The data-availability link appears to be only a placeholder GitHub URL, so the central annotated dataset, extracted metrics, and dataset list cannot actually be inspected or reused from the manuscript as given.

The literature search is too narrow for the breadth of the claimed field. The primary query requires only “large language model”/“llm” plus “citation”/“attribution”/“quote”, which risks missing work framed as grounded generation, source-grounded generation, evidence use, provenance, verification, or RAG without those exact terms.

The sensitivity analysis itself finds five additional relevant papers, but the authors do not incorporate them into the main corpus. Excluding known relevant studies because they do not alter the taxonomy undermines the completeness claims and can bias all reported counts and trends.

The paper repeatedly claims to be the first comprehensive survey of this paradigm, but the distinction from closely related citation, attribution, RAG, hallucination, and grounded-generation surveys is not argued sharply enough. The contribution often feels like relabeling and aggregating adjacent areas rather than providing a clearly new conceptual synthesis.

The taxonomy is descriptive but not deeply justified. Several categories are broad, overlapping, or operationally ambiguous, and the paper does not provide enough evidence that the proposed facets improve analysis beyond existing distinctions such as pre-hoc/post-hoc attribution, RAG, grounding, and citation generation.

Annotation reliability is only partially established. The full corpus was split between annotators rather than double annotated, agreement is measured on small random subsets, no agreement is available for parametric attribution, and some reported agreement values are based on labels appearing at least five times, which may hide instability for rarer but important categories.

Much of the analysis is count-based and surface-level. The manuscript reports percentages and temporal trends but offers limited critical synthesis of why methods succeed or fail, what assumptions underlie evaluation metrics, or how design choices causally affect reliability and user verification.

The paper’s main claims about unified benchmarks and fragmented evaluation are plausible, but the evidence is not always handled rigorously: metrics, frameworks, and datasets are catalogued, yet comparability, quality, and task-specific validity are not evaluated in much depth.

The manuscript has clarity and polish issues, including visible formatting/extraction artifacts in figures and incomplete-looking repository information. These issues make the paper feel less publication-ready and further weaken confidence in reproducibility.

Overall, the work has a potentially useful survey skeleton, but important revisions are needed to make the corpus complete and reproducible, sharpen the novelty, justify the taxonomy, and replace descriptive enumeration with stronger critical synthesis.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and central NLP problem: making LLM generations verifiable through attribution, citation, and quotation. The topic is clearly relevant to current work on hallucination, RAG, grounded generation, and trustworthy NLP systems.

The survey is broad and useful: 134 papers, 300 metrics, 19 frameworks, 231 datasets, and 11 benchmarks are organized into a coherent taxonomy. The distinction among attribution approach, citation characteristics, task, LLM integration, and evaluation dimensions gives readers a practical map of a fragmented area.

The methodology is substantially more rigorous than a typical narrative survey. The authors use a PRISMA-style process, define inclusion criteria, query multiple databases, report inter-annotator agreement, and include a sensitivity analysis of the search strategy.

The evaluation section is a particular strength. The paper does not merely list metrics; it classifies them by method and dimension, discusses when different dimensions should be used, and identifies the lack of shared benchmarks/frameworks as a concrete bottleneck for the field.

The manuscript is clearly written and well structured. The takeaways after each subsection help synthesize a large amount of literature, and the appendices provide useful detail for readers who want to inspect the underlying categorization.
weaknesses: The search strategy is quite narrow, relying primarily on title/abstract matches for “large language model” or “llm” combined with “citation”, “attribution”, or “quote”. The sensitivity analysis is helpful, but it was only run on ACL Anthology and arXiv and found five additional relevant papers that were not incorporated into the main corpus. This leaves some concern that the corpus underrepresents adjacent work framed as grounded generation, provenance, source linking, verifiable generation, or RAG faithfulness.

Reproducibility is weakened by the data availability presentation in the reviewed manuscript: the GitHub URL appears incomplete. Since many claims depend on the annotated paper/metric/dataset tables, the repository needs to be accessible and complete for the contribution to be fully reproducible.

The annotation process is credible but not fully double-coded. Screening and categorization were split between two annotators, with agreement measured only on samples. This is reasonable for scale, but some taxonomy boundaries are subjective, especially among attribution, citation style, task, and evaluation dimensions.

The paper is strongest as an organizing survey, but some parts remain descriptive. The taxonomy and metric guidelines are plausible, yet they are not externally validated through expert feedback, downstream use cases, or comparison against alternative taxonomies.

The claimed novelty as the first survey of the full paradigm is mostly convincing, but the relationship to existing RAG, attribution, grounding, and hallucination surveys could be sharpened further to make the unique contribution unmistakable to readers outside this subarea.
